*This is a submission for the [Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-weekend-2026-10-01)*

<!--
  [FRIEND STORY: replace this paragraph with the real version. Who is the friend (first name or nickname is fine),
  how you know them, and the actual evening that went wrong. Keep it short and specific: the city, the plan,
  the place that turned out to be closed or full, and one line they said afterwards.]
-->

[FRIEND] and I have the same argument every few weeks. Not a real argument. The "so where are we going?" kind.

[FRIEND] is the one who plans. I'm the one who says "anything is fine" and then has opinions later. Last time, [FRIEND] asked a chatbot for an evening: coffee first, then a museum, for two. It came back fast and sounded sure of itself. A nice café, a museum ten minutes away, a little paragraph about the vibe.

The museum was closed that day. [ADD THE REAL DETAIL: closed on that weekday / shut an hour earlier than it said / the café had moved.] Nobody had lied, exactly. The chatbot just filled the gaps with things that sounded right.

That is the part that stuck with me. Planning an evening isn't hard because there are no options. It's hard because you can't tell which details anyone actually checked.

So this weekend I built [FRIEND] a planner that is allowed to say "I don't know."

## What I Built

**Happen** turns one evening, described in your own words, into one checked plan.

You write something like:

> Coffee in Mexico City on Wednesday at 6 pm, then a museum, for two.

Happen does three things with it.

1. **Describe.** You type the evening like you'd text a friend.
2. **Review.** Happen turns it into a short brief: place, date, time, stop order, group size and budget. If something essential is missing, it asks you exactly one question. You can edit any field before anything is searched.
3. **Plan.** You press **Check live places**. Happen searches live listings, checks opening hours for *that* day against *your* time, and picks at most two stops.

**[ADD IMAGE: the landing page with a prompt typed in, desktop]**

Every stop shows its time, why it was picked, the listing details and one line that most planners never show you:

**Couldn't confirm.**

If the listing doesn't say whether a place takes reservations, Happen doesn't guess. If the hours for Wednesday are missing, that stop doesn't get the benefit of the doubt. Missing evidence never counts in a place's favour. That one rule is the whole product, really.

**[ADD IMAGE: a finished plan with two stops, showing the "Couldn't confirm" line]**

Then there's **View sources**. It opens what was checked, the planned day's opening hours (with the full week tucked behind a toggle), the source links grouped by type, and a full audit with the time each fact was retrieved. If [FRIEND] wants to know *why* the café made the cut, the answer is right there, with a link.

**[ADD IMAGE: the sources panel open, showing hours for the planned day and retrieval times]**

And if the plan isn't quite right, you type the change ("make the second stop something outdoors") and choose **Review this change**. Your current plan stays on screen until you press **Apply**. Nothing gets silently swapped out from under you.

### What it deliberately doesn't do

I cut a lot of things on purpose, and I'd rather say so than let a screenshot imply them:

- One evening, two stops at most.
- No travel time. The second stop shows its own opening hours and a directions link, not a made-up arrival time.
- No live crowd levels, reservations or price conversion.
- No accounts, no saved history, no database. Close the tab and it's gone.

A smaller plan that's true beats a bigger one you have to double-check yourself.

## Demo

**[ADD LIVE LINK: https://... ]**

**[ADD VIDEO: one evening, one follow-up question, one change. 60 to 90 seconds.]**

<!-- {% embed https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VIDEO_ID %} -->

**[ADD IMAGE: phone layout at 390px, showing the Plan / Brief / Sources switch]**

## Code

{% github kernelKain/happen %}

MIT licensed. Python backend (FastAPI), React and TypeScript frontend.

## How I Built It

Here's the path one evening takes:

```plaintext
"Coffee in Mexico City on Wednesday at 6 pm, then a museum, for two."
   │
   ▼
Brief  ── place, date, time, stop order, group size, budget
   │       (one question if something essential is missing)
   ▼
SerpApi ── Google Maps listings, official sites, community text
   │       (hard cap: 8 billed requests per plan, 15-minute cache)
   ▼
Python checks ── open on that day at that time?
   │              does the listing support what was asked for?
   │              missing evidence = no credit
   ▼
One plan, at most two stops
   ├── why each stop was chosen
   ├── one "Couldn't confirm" line per stop
   └── sources + audit with retrieval times
```

**SerpApi is the only data source.** Every fact on the screen traces back to a Google Maps listing, an official website or community text that SerpApi fetched. The server counts billed requests and refuses the ninth one before it is sent, so a single plan can never cost more than eight. A retry that actually reaches the network stays counted; a cancelled one costs nothing. Identical searches are cached for 15 minutes, so asking the same thing twice is free.

**Python makes the decision, not a model.** Scoring is plain code you can read. It checks feasibility (is this place open at 6 pm on a Wednesday?) and evidence (does anything actually say this place fits?). If two sources agree on the hours, that's agreement, not a conflict. If they disagree, you'll see it.

**Every claim carries its receipt.** Each fact in a plan has a source link and a retrieval time. The "Couldn't confirm" line is generated from whatever was *missing*, not from a template.

### Where the open model fits, and the result I didn't expect

This is the part I want to be upfront about, because it's the most interesting thing that happened this weekend.

The original design had **Gemma** reading the messy text, the community reviews and the user's prompt, and turning it into structured evidence that Python would then score. I picked Gemma 3 270M because it's small enough to run on a CPU on the same server as the API, with no GPU and no hosted inference. It runs locally through `llama.cpp` (`llama-cpp-python`), downloaded from a public quantized build, pinned to an exact revision and verified by SHA-256 before it loads. Temperature 0, fixed seed, so the same input gives the same output.

Then I did what you can only really do with an open model: I measured it myself, on my own task, before letting it near the product.

I wrote a held-out set (30 review excerpts, 24 planning prompts) and three gates the model had to pass before any of its output could reach a user:

| Gate | Required | Gemma 3 270M | Gemma 3 1B |
|---|---|---|---|
| Valid JSON on review extraction | 95% | **6.7%** (2 of 30) | 100% |
| Right dimension and polarity on reviews | 80% | **4.4%** | 67.8% |
| Valid JSON on planning prompts | 95% | 91.7% | 100% |
| Essential planning fields correct | 90% | 66.7% | 79.2% |

The 270M model mostly couldn't produce valid JSON for my schema. The 1B model was a big step up, fit in about 1.3 GB of memory and loaded in under a second, but it still got the review polarity wrong about a third of the time. For a product whose entire promise is "we only tell you what we checked," a model that's wrong a third of the time about whether a review is positive is worse than no model.

So the model ships **gated off**, and the gate is code, not a promise. There's a checked-in quality report (`ml/reports/model-quality.json`). At startup the backend hashes the model file and compares it to the hash in that report. Model-derived claims are only allowed if the report for *that exact file* says it passed. Right now it says it didn't, so a deterministic parser reads the prompt instead, and the health endpoint openly reports `model_claims_enabled: false`.

I'll be honest: I wanted to write "Gemma powers Happen." It would have made a better headline. But building a tool about not overclaiming and then overclaiming in the post felt wrong. What I can say is that the open model shaped the design. It's the reason there's a schema, a validator, a held-out set and a gate at all, and the moment a Gemma model clears those gates, turning it on is a config change.

### How I worked

I built this over the weekend with an AI coding agent as a pair. I wrote a product contract first (what it does, what it must never claim, the request budget), and every change was checked against it. I used **Entire** to checkpoint the agent sessions into the git history, so the reasoning behind each commit lives next to the code.

What the test suite covers right now:

- 466 backend tests, all with mocks and captured fixtures. They never spend a SerpApi credit.
- 68 frontend unit tests.
- 22 Playwright tests at 1280px and 390px, with automated accessibility checks (axe) on every one.
- A secret scanner over the whole tree, and a check of the production bundle for keys, hosts and test fixtures.

One bug I'm a little proud of catching: a typed follow-up answer was occasionally cleared before it was sent. It failed about 1 run in 28, and never when the test ran alone on an idle machine. I only found it by running the suite dozens of times and tallying the failures. After the fix it passed 40 runs in a row, and the test now checks that the typed answer actually arrives in the request body, so it can't sneak back in.

## Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

**Because I could check the model instead of trusting it.** With open weights I downloaded the exact file, pinned its hash, ran it on my own laptop with the Wi-Fi off and scored it against my own task. A closed API would have given me a nice demo and a changelog. It wouldn't have let me prove, file by file, that the thing in production is the thing I tested. And it couldn't have told me so clearly that the model wasn't ready.

**Because "no" was an option.** With a hosted model, the model *is* the product, and if it's not good enough you're stuck. Here, the open model is one swappable piece behind a gate. When the 270M model failed, I tried the 1B by changing a few lines of config. When a bigger Gemma clears the bar, it's the same change again. No vendor, no new contract, no new API key.

**Because it costs nothing to run.** The model runs on the same CPU as the API. There's no per-token bill, which matters for something I want to hand to a friend and leave running.

**Because the evidence trail is open too.** The scoring, the request cap, the quality report and the gate are all in the repo. If you don't believe a plan, you can read exactly how it was made.

What did open lose? Quality, at this size. A large hosted model would probably have passed my gates on day one. But I'd have had no way to keep checking it, and no way to know when it quietly changed.

title: Arun plans every evening like a research paper. So I built him a planner that is allowed to say it doesn't know.
published: false
tags: devchallenge, weekendchallenge, hf26challenge, opensource
cover_image: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kernelKain/happen/main/docs/press/cover.png
---

*This is a submission for the [Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-weekend-2026-10-01)*

Arun is the friend who plans. I am the friend who says "anything is fine" and then has opinions later.

He does it the same way every time. Ten Google Maps tabs. A screenshot of opening hours that might be last year's. A chatbot paragraph that sounds finished. Last month he asked one for drinks in Lisbon, for two, around nine. It came back in seconds: three bars, a little note about the lighting, a walking time that nobody had measured. One of those bars was closed that weekday. Arun still showed up, because the answer had sounded sure of itself.

That is the part that stuck with me. Planning an evening is not hard because there are no options. It is hard because you cannot tell which details anyone actually checked.

So this weekend I built him a planner that is allowed to say "I don't know."

## What I Built

**Happen** turns one evening, written in your own words, into one checked plan.

You write something like:

> Drinks in Lisbon on Friday at 9 for two.

Happen does three things with it.

1. **Describe.** You type the evening like you would text Arun.
2. **Review.** Happen turns it into a short brief: place, date, time, stop order, group size. If something essential is missing, it asks exactly one question. You can edit any field before anything is searched.
3. **Plan.** You press **Check live places**. Happen searches live listings, checks opening hours for *that* day against *your* time, and picks at most two stops.

![Happen landing: type an evening, or pick a starter like drinks in Lisbon](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kernelKain/happen/main/docs/press/landing.png)
*The landing. One box, three starter evenings, and three promises: live listings, feasibility first, no hidden guesses.*

The review step is there so Arun can catch a bad parse before SerpApi spends a credit. His words stay on the left. What Happen will actually check sits on the right.

![Review step before any search: the brief on the left, what happens next on the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kernelKain/happen/main/docs/press/review.png)
*Review. Nothing has been searched yet. "Check live places" is the first billed step.*

Every stop then shows its time, why it was picked, the listing details, and one line most planners never show you:

**Couldn't confirm.**

If the listing does not say whether a place has seating for two, Happen does not guess. If Wednesday's hours are missing, that stop does not get the benefit of the doubt. Missing evidence never counts in a place's favour. That one rule is the whole product.

![A finished Lisbon plan: Ágave Cocktail Lab at 9pm, open, with one Couldn’t confirm line](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kernelKain/happen/main/docs/press/plan.png)
*Arun's Wednesday in Lisbon. One stop, open at 9. Couldn't confirm: price, current crowd level, or seating for two.*

**View sources** opens what was checked, the planned day's hours, the source links, and a full audit with the time each fact was retrieved. If Arun wants to know why Ágave made the cut, the answer is a link, not a vibe paragraph.

And if the plan is not quite right, he types the change and chooses **Review this change**. The current plan stays on screen until he presses **Apply**. Nothing gets swapped out from under him.

### What it deliberately doesn't do

I cut a lot of things on purpose, and I would rather say so than let a screenshot imply them:

- One evening, two stops at most.
- No travel time. A second stop shows its own hours and a directions link, not a made-up arrival.
- No live crowd levels, reservations, or price conversion. Those three are exactly what the Lisbon plan refused to invent.
- No accounts, no saved history, no database. Close the tab and it is gone.

A smaller plan that is true beats a bigger one you have to double-check yourself.

## Demo

**Try it:** [happen-web.onrender.com](https://happen-web.onrender.com/)

Type an evening, or tap one of the starters. **Drinks in Lisbon on Friday at 9 for two** is the one in the screenshots.

No login. The first search spends live SerpApi credits. Asking the same evening again within 15 minutes does not.

## Code

{% github kernelKain/happen %}

MIT licensed. Python backend (FastAPI), React and TypeScript frontend.

## How I Built It

Here is the path one evening takes:

```plaintext
"Drinks in Lisbon on Friday at 9 for two."
   │
   ▼
Brief  ── place, date, time, stop order, group size
   │       (one question if something essential is missing)
   ▼
SerpApi ── Google Maps listings, official sites, community text
   │       (hard cap: 8 billed requests per plan, 15-minute cache)
   ▼
Python checks ── open on that day at that time?
   │              does the listing support what was asked for?
   │              missing evidence = no credit
   ▼
One plan, at most two stops
   ├── why each stop was chosen
   ├── one "Couldn't confirm" line per stop
   └── sources + audit with retrieval times
```

**SerpApi is the only data source.** Every fact on the screen traces back to a Google Maps listing, an official website, or community text that SerpApi fetched. The server counts billed requests and refuses the ninth one before it is sent, so a single plan can never cost more than eight. A retry that actually reaches the network stays counted. A cancelled one costs nothing. Identical searches are cached for 15 minutes.

**Python makes the decision, not a model.** Scoring is plain code you can read. It checks feasibility (is this place open at 9pm on a Wednesday?) and evidence (does anything actually say this place fits?). If two sources agree on the hours, that is agreement, not a conflict. If they disagree, you will see it.

**Every claim carries its receipt.** Each fact has a source link and a retrieval time. The "Couldn't confirm" line is generated from whatever was *missing*, not from a template. On Arun's Lisbon plan that line is price, crowd, and seating for two, because the listings never said those things.

### Where the open model fits, and the result I did not expect

This is the part I want to be upfront about, because it is the most interesting thing that happened this weekend.

The original design had **Gemma** reading the messy text, the community reviews, and the user's prompt, and turning it into structured evidence that Python would then score. I picked Gemma 3 270M because it is small enough to run on a CPU on the same server as the API, with no GPU and no hosted inference. It runs locally through `llama.cpp`, downloaded from a public quantized build, pinned to an exact revision and verified by SHA-256 before it loads. Temperature 0, fixed seed, so the same input gives the same output.

Then I did what you can only really do with an open model: I measured it myself, on my own task, before letting it near the product.

I wrote a held-out set (30 review excerpts, 24 planning prompts) and three gates the model had to pass before any of its output could reach a user:

| Gate | Required | Gemma 3 270M | Gemma 3 1B |
|---|---|---|---|
| Valid JSON on review extraction | 95% | **6.7%** (2 of 30) | 100% |
| Right dimension and polarity on reviews | 80% | **4.4%** | 67.8% |
| Valid JSON on planning prompts | 95% | 91.7% | 100% |
| Essential planning fields correct | 90% | 66.7% | 79.2% |

The 270M model mostly could not produce valid JSON for my schema. So I tried to fix it the way open weights let you: I wrote 100 training examples (no text shared with the held-out set) and trained a short QLoRA adapter on a free Colab T4. It came back at 6.7% parse and 3.3% accuracy, *worse* than the untuned model. My rule was that an adapter only ships if it beats the baseline by five points without more invalid output, so it did not ship. At that point, with about eight hours left, I asked my agent whether I should pivot the whole project. The answer was no: the product was already built to refuse when evidence is thin, so a weak model makes it quieter, not wrong.

The 1B model was a big step up. It fit in about 1.3 GB of memory and loaded in under a second, but it still got the review polarity wrong about a third of the time. For a product whose entire promise is "we only tell you what we checked," a model that is wrong a third of the time about whether a review is positive is worse than no model.

So the model ships **gated off**, and the gate is code, not a promise. There is a checked-in quality report (`ml/reports/model-quality.json`). At startup the backend hashes the model file and compares it to the hash in that report. Model-derived claims are only allowed if the report for *that exact file* says it passed. Right now it says it did not, so a deterministic parser reads the prompt instead, and the health endpoint openly reports `model_claims_enabled: false`.

I wanted to write "Gemma powers Happen." It would have made a better headline. Building a tool about not overclaiming, and then overclaiming in the post, felt wrong. What I can say is that the open model shaped the design. It is the reason there is a schema, a validator, a held-out set, and a gate at all. The moment a Gemma model clears those gates, turning it on is a config change.

### How I worked

I built this over the weekend in Cursor, with Grok 4.7 High as my coding agent. I wrote a product contract first (what it does, what it must never claim, the request budget), and every change was checked against it.

I used **Entire** to checkpoint the agent sessions into the git history, so the reasoning behind each commit lives next to the code. The public session log is here: [entire.io/gh/kernelKain/happen/sessions](https://entire.io/gh/kernelKain/happen/sessions).

![Entire dashboard for Happen: 31 checkpoints, 8 PRs merged, token usage over the weekend](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kernelKain/happen/main/docs/press/entire.png)
*The weekend on Entire. 31 checkpoints across 62 commits, 8 PRs merged, about 5.7 million tokens. The spike is October 4, when the live planner and the evidence-first UI landed.*

What the test suite covers right now:

- 466 backend tests, all with mocks and captured fixtures. They never spend a SerpApi credit.
- 68 frontend unit tests.
- 22 Playwright tests at 1280px and 390px, with automated accessibility checks (axe) on every one.
- A secret scanner over the whole tree, and a check of the production bundle for keys, hosts, and test fixtures.

One bug I am a little proud of catching: a typed follow-up answer was occasionally cleared before it was sent. It failed about 1 run in 28, and never when the test ran alone on an idle machine. I only found it by running the suite dozens of times and tallying the failures. After the fix it passed 40 runs in a row, and the test now checks that the typed answer actually arrives in the request body, so it cannot sneak back in.

## Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

**Because I could check the model instead of trusting it.** With open weights I downloaded the exact file, pinned its hash, ran it on my own laptop, and scored it against my own task. A closed API would have given me a nice demo and a changelog. It would not have let me prove, file by file, that the thing in production is the thing I tested. And it could not have told me so clearly that the model was not ready.

**Because "no" was an option.** With a hosted model, the model *is* the product, and if it is not good enough you are stuck. Here, the open model is one swappable piece behind a gate. When the 270M model failed, I tried the 1B by changing a few lines of config. When a bigger Gemma clears the bar, it is the same change again. No vendor, no new contract, no new API key.

**Because it costs nothing to run.** The model runs on the same CPU as the API. There is no per-token bill, which matters for something I want to hand to a friend and leave running.

**Because the evidence trail is open too.** The scoring, the request cap, the quality report, and the gate are all in the repo. If you do not believe a plan, you can read exactly how it was made.

What did open lose? Quality, at this size. A large hosted model would probably have passed my gates on day one. But I would have had no way to keep checking it, and no way to know when it quietly changed.

## Handing It Over

I sent Arun the live URL and asked him to plan the Lisbon evening himself. He typed the prompt, fixed nothing on the review screen, and pressed **Check live places**.

He read the Ágave card twice. The first thing he pointed at was not the 5-star rating. It was the last line.

> "Okay. So it is open at 9, and it is not pretending it knows the price. That is actually useful. I keep getting paragraphs. I wanted the gap."

He understood the difference without me explaining it. **Why it fits** is what the listings supported: hours at 9, an official site, a Maps rating. **Couldn't confirm** is what they did not: price, how busy it is right now, seating for two. He said he would still go, and that he would text the bar about a table, which is the decision Happen is supposed to leave with him.

The part that confused him was the single stop. He expected a second place "because the landing said up to two." I told him the honest version: a second stop only appears if a second place also clears the hours check. Happen will not pad the evening to look complete. He said that should be on the result, not only in my head. Fair. If I change one line of copy after this weekend, it is that one.

## My Agent Session

I made the product calls: two stops at most, missing evidence never helps a place, eight requests per plan, and shipping the model gated off rather than pretending. The agent wrote and tested most of the code against that contract.

The session I would point a judge to is the one where the model failed. It walks through running the QLoRA notebook on a free Colab T4, getting 6.7% parse and 3.3% accuracy back, and then asking, with eight hours left, whether I should throw the project away. The answer was to keep the refusal behaviour, stop tuning, and ship the deploy.

The full checkpoint trail is on Entire: [entire.io/gh/kernelKain/happen/sessions](https://entire.io/gh/kernelKain/happen/sessions).

## Prize Categories

- **Best Use of SerpApi.** SerpApi is the only data source in Happen. Google Maps listings, official websites, and community text all come through it, and every fact in a plan links back to the SerpApi result it came from, with a retrieval time. The server enforces a hard budget of eight billed requests per plan (the ninth is refused before it is sent) and caches identical searches for 15 minutes.
- **Best Use of Entire.** Agent sessions were checkpointed with Entire throughout the build. The public log is [here](https://entire.io/gh/kernelKain/happen/sessions). This weekend: 31 checkpoints, 8 merged PRs, the reasoning sitting next to the commits.
- **Best Use of Render.** The live app is [happen-web.onrender.com](https://happen-web.onrender.com/). Frontend as a static site, backend as a Python web service in Singapore, both defined in `render.yaml` and deployed from `main` only after checks pass. The SerpApi key lives in the Render dashboard, never in the repo. The backend build downloads the pinned Gemma file and verifies its hash on Render, with no Hugging Face token and no hosted inference.

---

*Built for Arun, who will now have one fewer reason to open ten Maps tabs and still pick the usual place.*
